newsitem.title: SYRIA: Syria's Assad says doesn't rule out Israeli attack.
newsitem.headline: Syria's Assad says doesn't rule out Israeli attack.

text.p: Syrian President Hafez al-Assad said on Monday he did not rule out the possibility of an Israeli attack against Syria or Lebanon and accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of working against peace.

Asked at a joint news conference with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak whether he ruled out an Israeli attack against Syria or south Lebanon, Assad said: "This should not happen, but nobody could say that it will not happen. It is a possibility."
Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy swiftly reacted to Assad's comments, saying the Jewish state had no intention of attacking Syria.
"Israel has said time and again, through the various channels and also in public that it has no intention of attacking Syria," Levy told Israel radio.
"On the contrary it (Israel) is interested in reducing the level of tension and creating an atmosphere conducive to renewing peace talks," Levy said.

Syria's redeployment of some 12,000 troops in Lebanon in September, which included movement of some units to within striking distance of a key Israeli position on the Golan Heights, spurred war jitters in Israel.
Mubarak told the Damascus news conference that the Syrian manoeuvres should not be taken as preparation for war.

"I want to add to what my brother Hafez said that regarding the exercises which they (Israelis) talked about...all world armies conduct manoeuvres and this does not mean that training is a preparation for a military operation," Mubarak said.

"When we conducted manoeuvres at the beginning of 1996 there was a big fuss. When Israel's president visited me there was a big air manoeuvre in Israel and after it a massive manoeuvre in the Golan. We did not bother. This is ordinary. Training is an ordinary thing," he added.
Israeli security sources said last Monday that Israel's defence chiefs had told Netanyahu the army needed more than $1 billion because of an increased chance of war with Syria.

During the news conference Assad praised efforts exerted by U.S. President Bill Clinton to advance the Arab-Israeli peace talks but added that the process was slowed by the campign for the November 5 U.S. presidential election.
"In meetings and contacts which have occurred during these years between myself and Clinton I had the feeling that he was enthusiastic and serious for pushing the peace process forward," Assad said.

"I think the election...slowed this activity and I cannot say how the matter will be (after the election), but I can say that President Clinton has been honest in dealing with the peace process during the recent years," he added.
Syria has held sporadic peace talks with Israel since 1991, but no negotiations have been held since before Netanyahu came to power in June.
Syria and Arabs have strongly rejected Netanyahu's refusal to trade the occupied Arab lands for peace. Syria wants Israel to withdraw fully from the Golan, occupied by Israel since 1967.
Mubarak, who returned home after the news conference, said no preparations were being made for an Arab summit and that the issue was not discussed during his talks with Assad.
